metadata.title: Neuron-Enhanced AutoEncoder Matrix Completion and Collaborative Filtering: Theory and Practice
metadata.authors: Jicong Fan, Rui Chen, Zhao Zhang, Chris H.Q. Ding

section.title: Introduction
section.summary: The section motivates collaborative filtering and missing data imputation with highly incomplete matrices. It argues that existing autoencoder-based collaborative filtering methods use a linear decoder output and may not capture nonlinear response functions. It states the paper's contributions: AEMC-NE, generalization analysis under MCAR and MNAR, and experiments on synthetic and benchmark datasets.

item.text: Recover missing entries in rating or data matrices where missing rates can be very high.
Existing autoencoder matrix completion methods usually use a linear output activation, implying linear interactions between learned features at the output.
The proposed element-wise network adaptively learns an output activation function to approximate nonlinear response functions.
The paper claims theoretical analysis covers both missing completely at random and missing not at random settings.
Experiments are stated for synthetic data, MovieLens-100k, MovieLens-1M, MovieLens-10M, Douban, and Flixster.

section.title: Neuron-Enhanced AEMC
section.summary: This section formulates autoencoder matrix completion and introduces AEMC-NE. AEMC-NE composes a main autoencoder with a shared element-wise neural network that learns the output activation function. The section also discusses MNAR weighting, optimization, and time and space complexity.

item.text: Matrix completion is formulated as minimizing observed-entry reconstruction loss over a function class.
AEMC is defined as an autoencoder with a linear output layer and Frobenius weight regularization.
AEMC-NE replaces the fixed output activation with a learned element-wise neural network h composed with the main network g.
The element-wise network is shared across all output entries and learns an adaptive activation function.
For MNAR, the paper suggests replacing the binary observation mask S with weights Q based on estimated observation probabilities.
The network architecture cannot be easily adapted for new users because the output layer size must be changed; the cold-start problem is not considered.

section.title: Theoretical Guarantee
section.summary: This section derives generalization bounds for AEMC-NE under MCAR and MNAR. The MCAR theorem bounds missing-entry loss by observed-entry loss plus complexity and concentration terms. The section interprets the bounds as supporting the element-wise network, zero filling, and improved bounds when the sample dimension grows.

item.text: Under MCAR, the paper bounds the difference between loss on missing entries and loss on observed entries for AEMC-NE.
The element-wise network can reduce the generalization error upper bound when its training-error reduction exceeds its added complexity.
Zero filling can yield a smaller bound term involving the Frobenius norm of the temporarily imputed matrix than other weak filling methods.
With fixed sampling rate and network structure, increasing the number of samples tightens the bound, and a larger difference between numbers of variables and samples can help.
Under MNAR with entry-specific observation probabilities, the paper provides a propensity-weighted generalization bound.

section.title: Connection with Previous Work
section.summary: This section relates the element-wise network to adaptive activation functions and contrasts the theoretical setting with prior generalization analyses. It also compares the paper's bound with a nuclear-norm matrix completion bound from Shamir and Shalev-Shwartz.

item.text: The element-wise neural network can be viewed as an adaptive activation function learned from data.
Adaptive activation methods using piecewise polynomials are discussed as related work.
The paper compares its bound to a nuclear norm minimization collaborative filtering bound.
The paper states that when n is sufficiently large, its bound can be tighter than the nuclear-norm bound under the discussed conditions.

section.title: Numerical Results
section.summary: This section reports experiments on synthetic data and collaborative filtering benchmarks. It evaluates AEMC-NE against AEMC variants and multiple collaborative filtering baselines using relative recovery error and RMSE. It also includes an additional MovieLens-1M subset experiment linked to the theory about tall or fat matrices.

item.text: Synthetic matrix of size 300 by 3000 generated from a 10-dimensional nonlinear latent variable model; MCAR and MNAR settings are tested.
Synthetic experiments use relative recovery error; collaborative filtering experiments use RMSE.
AEMC-NE has lower relative recovery error than AEMC in all reported MNAR synthetic missing-rate cases.
MovieLens-100k, MovieLens-1M, and MovieLens-10M are evaluated with 90 percent of known ratings for training and 10 percent for testing.
AEMC-NE reports RMSE 0.8767 on ML-100k, 0.8248 on ML-1M, and 0.7723 on ML-10M.
AEMC-NE reports RMSE 0.7286 on Douban and 0.8816 on Flixster.

section.title: Conclusion
section.summary: The conclusion restates AEMC-NE as a collaborative filtering method with a layer-wise network and an element-wise network. It summarizes that the paper provides generalization bounds and experimental comparisons. It also states possible extensions to implicit feedback and general missing data imputation.

item.text: AEMC-NE uses an element-wise network to learn an adaptive output activation function.
The paper states that its theoretical bounds verify the effectiveness of AEMC-NE.
The conclusion states that AEMC-NE outperformed many baselines on collaborative filtering benchmarks.
The method can be extended to implicit feedback by using negative sampling and ranking losses such as BPR loss.
AEMC-NE is stated to be applicable to more general missing data imputation problems.

section.title: Appendices
section.summary: The appendices provide an MNAR theorem with estimated propensities, network-structure comparisons, synthetic data details, hyperparameter analyses, runtime and NDCG results, MNAR MovieLens experiments, UCI missing-data imputation experiments, and proofs. They include additional tables and figures supporting the main text.

item.text: An MNAR bound is provided for estimated propensities and includes an additional error term for propensity estimation.
AEMC-NE is related to an AEMC variant with additional decoder layers but sparse and shared weights.
UCI Breast, Letter, Credit, and News datasets are used for missing-data imputation with 20 percent missing rate.
NDCG@1, NDCG@5, NDCG@10, and NDCG@50 are reported for MovieLens-100k and MovieLens-1M.
AEMC-NE has higher NDCG than AEMC in all reported MovieLens NDCG cases.
AEMC-NE runtime is higher than AEMC on all five listed datasets.

claims.item: AEMC-NE learns an element-wise output activation to approximate nonlinear response functions in matrix completion and collaborative filtering.
Theorem 3.1 gives an MCAR generalization bound comparing missing-entry and observed-entry losses.
Theorem 3.2 gives an MNAR propensity-weighted generalization bound.
Theoretical discussion states that the element-wise network, zero filling, and larger sample dimension can improve the bound under specified conditions.
The method's element-wise network is connected to adaptive activation functions.
Theorem A.1 extends the MNAR analysis to estimated propensities.

method_components.item: Observed-entry reconstruction objective for autoencoder matrix completion.
Main autoencoder g_W maps the temporarily imputed matrix to reconstructed entries.
Shared element-wise network h_Theta learns the decoder output activation.
Frobenius weight regularization is applied to both main and element-wise networks.
MNAR variant can weight observed entries by estimated inverse observation probabilities.
AEMC-NE is optimized with gradient-based optimizers such as Adam.

datasets.item: Synthetic 300 by 3000 matrix from nonlinear latent variable model.
Douban and Flixster preprocessed subsets with 3000 users and 3000 items.
UCI Breast, Letter, Credit, and News datasets.

baselines.item: AEMC or AutoRec and AEMC with ReLU output.
AEMC+, AEMC++, and AEMC+-NE variants in synthetic or subset experiments.
MovieLens baselines include BiasMF, NNMF, LLORMA, GC-MC, AutoSVD++, AutoSVD, CF-NADE, DMF+, IMC-GAE, and GHRS.
Douban and Flixster baselines include PMF, GRALS, sRGCNN, GC-MC, Factorized EAE, and GRAEM.
UCI imputation baselines include MissForest, MICE, EM, Auto-encoder, and GAIN.

ablations.item: Synthetic experiments compare AEMC-NE with AEMC, AEMC+, and AEMC++.
Synthetic analyses vary missing rate, element-wise network width, main-network middle-layer width, and weight decay.
MovieLens-1M subset compares AEMC-NE with SVD, SVD++, AEMC, AEMC+, and AEMC++.
Appendix D varies hidden units in the main and element-wise networks on MovieLens-1M.

metrics.item: Relative recovery error for synthetic matrix completion.
NDCG@1, NDCG@5, NDCG@10, and NDCG@50 for MovieLens ranking evaluation.
Runtime in seconds for AEMC and AEMC-NE.

results.item: On synthetic MCAR data, AEMC-NE is reported to outperform AEMC and deeper AEMC variants across missing rates in Figure 2.
On synthetic MNAR data, AEMC-NE has lower relative recovery error than AEMC for missing rates 0.2 through 0.7 in Table 1.
On MovieLens, AEMC-NE reports RMSE 0.8767, 0.8248, and 0.7723 for ML-100k, ML-1M, and ML-10M respectively.
On Douban and Flixster, AEMC-NE reports RMSE 0.7286 and 0.8816 respectively.
On the MovieLens-1M subset, AEMC-NE reports RMSE 0.8182, lower than SVD, SVD++, AEMC, AEMC+, and AEMC++ in Table 4.
AEMC-NE reports higher runtime than AEMC and higher NDCG than AEMC in appendix experiments.

stated_limitations.item: The AEMC-NE architecture cannot be easily adapted for new users because the main output layer size changes.
The paper states it is not considering the cold-start problem.
The paper notes that improvements over linear models are not very significant on square or nearly square rating matrices.
The paper considers explicit feedback in the reported collaborative filtering experiments and states implicit feedback would require negative sampling and ranking losses such as BPR.
